Class 1

The Space Between Profit and Purpose

Defining what social entrepreneurship is — and sharpening the line against what it is not

Imagine two cafés on the same block in Tiong Bahru, Singapore. Both serve exceptional single-origin coffee. Both turn a profit. But in the first, the barista behind the machine is a formerly incarcerated woman completing a twelve-month training programme that will certify her as a specialty coffee professional. In the second, the barista is a design graduate pulling latte art for Instagram. The coffee tastes the same. The price is the same. The customer experience may be indistinguishable. Yet something fundamentally different is happening in the first café — something that changes how we should evaluate its success, structure its financing, and judge its leadership decisions.

That first café is Bettr Barista, one of Singapore's most visible social enterprises. And the question this chapter poses is deceptively simple: what exactly makes it different? Not different in a feel-good, marketing-copy sense — but structurally, strategically, and ethically different in ways that demand a distinct framework for understanding.

Why Definitions Matter More Than You Think

You are reading this chapter as someone who already has a startup running or in formation. You carry intuitions about social entrepreneurship — gleaned from pitch competitions, TED talks, impact investing newsletters, or the origin stories of ventures you admire. Those intuitions are valuable. But they are almost certainly imprecise, and imprecision in this domain has consequences.

When definitions are fuzzy, several things go wrong. Funders cannot distinguish between a company with a genuine social mission and one that has learned to speak the language of impact. Policymakers design support schemes that either include too much (subsidising commercially viable businesses that would exist anyway) or too little (excluding innovative models that do not fit bureaucratic categories). And founders — people like you — make strategic decisions without clarity about which goal takes priority when profit and purpose collide.

The scholarly literature on social entrepreneurship has been remarkably candid about this problem. A systematic review of 395 articles in top-tier journals concluded that social entrepreneurship "remains an unclear and contested concept" (Saebi et al., 2018, p. 75). An integrative review spanning decades of research confirmed that "the term 'social entrepreneurship' has no universally agreed-upon definition" (Klarin & Suseno, 2023). This is not a failure of the field — it reflects the genuine complexity of organisations that straddle logics that the modern economy has kept separate for centuries.

But the absence of a universal definition does not mean all definitions are equally useful. This chapter will equip you with a working definition sharp enough to guide decisions, a spectrum model flexible enough to capture real-world variety, and a tension framework honest enough to prepare you for the hardest choices you will face.

What Social Entrepreneurship Is

The intellectual foundation of the field rests on a deceptively elegant idea articulated by J. Gregory Dees in what remains the most cited paper in social entrepreneurship scholarship. Dees (1998/2001) argued that social entrepreneurs are change agents in the social sector who combine five qualities: they adopt a mission to create and sustain social value (not just private value); they relentlessly pursue new opportunities to serve that mission; they engage in continuous innovation, adaptation, and learning; they act boldly without being limited by resources currently in hand; and they exhibit heightened accountability to the constituencies they serve and for the outcomes they create.

Notice what this definition does and does not say. It does not mention profit. It does not require a specific legal structure. It does not demand that the organisation earn revenue from the market. What it insists upon is mission primacy — the social mission is not a byproduct of the venture but its organising logic.

Austin, Stevenson, and Wei-Skillern (2006) built on this foundation by systematically comparing social and commercial entrepreneurship. Their analysis identified four key variables that differentiate the two: market failure (social entrepreneurs operate where markets have failed to serve a population), mission (which is central rather than instrumental), resource mobilisation (which often relies on non-market mechanisms like grants, volunteers, and subsidies), and performance measurement (which must capture social outcomes that resist quantification).

Mair and Martí (2006) added a crucial process dimension, defining social entrepreneurship as "the innovative use and combination of resources to pursue opportunities to catalyse social change and/or address social needs" (p. 37). Their framing emphasises that social entrepreneurship is not a type of organisation but a type of activity — one that can occur inside nonprofits, businesses, cooperatives, or government agencies.

Think About It

Before reading on, consider your own venture. Which of Dees's five qualities does it embody most strongly? Which feels weakest? If a sceptical investor asked you, "How is this different from a regular startup with a nice mission statement?" — what would you say?

Drawing the Boundaries: What Social Entrepreneurship Is Not

A working definition gains its power as much from what it excludes as from what it includes. Three adjacent concepts frequently blur into social entrepreneurship, and separating them is essential.

Social entrepreneurship is not corporate social responsibility (CSR). CSR is the practice of an established, profit-primary corporation integrating social and environmental considerations into its operations. When DBS Bank funds community programmes or Singtel runs digital literacy workshops, these are valuable contributions — but the corporation's core logic remains shareholder value. As Mair and Martí (2006) note, CSR "remains profit-primary" and lacks the mission centrality that defines social entrepreneurship. The social activity is subordinate to the commercial engine.

Social entrepreneurship is not charity or traditional philanthropy. Charities address social needs through the redistribution of donated resources. What distinguishes social entrepreneurship is its market orientation — the use of earned revenue, entrepreneurial strategy, and business discipline to pursue social outcomes. A food bank distributes donated groceries. A social enterprise might train and employ marginalised individuals to grow, cook, and sell meals — using the market mechanism itself as the vehicle for impact.

Social entrepreneurship is not simply a conventional startup that happens to do some good. This is the most seductive confusion. A ride-hailing platform that creates economic opportunities for drivers is doing something positive — but if its strategic decisions are governed by growth metrics, investor returns, and market share rather than by a defined social mission, it operates within commercial logic. The distinction, as Saebi et al. (2018) argue, lies in the dual mission: the simultaneous, intentional pursuit of both social and economic value creation as core objectives.

The Social Enterprise Spectrum

If the boundaries between social entrepreneurship and its neighbours are clearer now, the territory within those boundaries remains vast. Not all social enterprises look alike, and a binary classification — social or not social — misses the rich variety of models that exist in practice.

This is why the social enterprise spectrum is such a useful conceptual tool. Picture a horizontal continuum. At the far left sits the purely commercial enterprise: its sole purpose is to generate financial returns for owners and shareholders. At the far right sits the purely philanthropic organisation: it creates social value through donated resources with no expectation of financial return. Everything in between represents some hybrid of commercial and social logic.

Defourny and Nyssens (2010) mapped how this spectrum manifests differently across institutional contexts. In the United States, the social enterprise tradition grew from nonprofits seeking earned-income strategies — moving rightward organisations toward the centre by adding commercial discipline. In Europe, social enterprises emerged from the cooperative and welfare-state tradition, emphasising democratic governance and multi-stakeholder participation. In Southeast Asia, and particularly in Singapore, the spectrum reflects a different heritage again — one shaped by a developmental state, a pragmatic policy culture, and a relatively young but rapidly professionalising social sector.

The spectrum is not a ranking. Being closer to the "social" end does not make an organisation morally superior, nor does proximity to the "commercial" end make it suspect. The spectrum is a descriptive tool that helps us understand how an organisation balances its dual commitments and where specific tensions are likely to arise.

Singapore Ventures Along the Spectrum

Consider three Singapore-based social enterprises, each occupying a different position on the spectrum:

Bettr Barista operates a specialty coffee academy and cafés that employ and train marginalised women and at-risk youth. Its commercial operations — selling coffee, running barista courses — generate the revenue that funds its social programme. The business model is designed so that every cup sold directly sustains the training pipeline. This is a tightly integrated model: the commercial activity and the social mission are the same activity.

Foreword Coffee runs a café chain staffed significantly by persons with disabilities and from disadvantaged backgrounds. Like Bettr Barista, the commercial vehicle (coffee) is the social vehicle (inclusive employment). But the emphasis on disability inclusion means Foreword navigates additional operational complexities — workplace adaptations, training timelines, and customer education — that create distinct mission-market pressures.

Adrenalin Group empowers at-risk youth through creative industries — media production, events, and content creation. Here the social mission (youth development) is pursued through commercial projects (media production for paying clients), but the client-facing deliverables and the beneficiary outcomes are partially separable. A client cares about the quality of the video produced; Adrenalin cares about what the process of producing it did for the young person involved.

Each of these ventures would place at a different point on the spectrum, and each faces a different version of the central tension that defines the field.

Think About It

Where would you intuitively place your own venture on a spectrum from pure commercial to pure social mission? What sits to your left and right — what kinds of organisations share your approximate position? What does that neighbourhood tell you about the pressures you are likely to face?

The Double Bottom Line

If the spectrum describes where a social enterprise sits, the double bottom line describes what it is accountable for. The concept is straightforward: unlike a conventional business (which measures success by financial performance) or a traditional charity (which measures success by social outcomes), a social enterprise must deliver on both simultaneously.

The term gained institutional weight in Singapore through raiSE, the Singapore Centre for Social Enterprise. Established in 2015 through collaboration between the Ministry of Social and Family Development, the National Council of Social Service, and the Social Enterprise Association, raiSE defines social enterprises as "business entities set up with clear social goals; and where there is clear management intent and resources allocated to fulfil their social objectives" (raiSE, n.d.). Crucially, raiSE membership requires a commitment to the double bottom line: financial returns and social impact.

This sounds elegant in a pitch deck. In practice, it is a source of relentless tension. The double bottom line means that every significant decision — pricing, hiring, product development, expansion, partnerships — must be evaluated against two criteria that frequently pull in opposite directions. Hire the most qualified candidate, or the candidate whose life trajectory the role would most transform? Price the product to maximise margin, or to ensure accessibility for the community you serve? Accept the corporate contract that boosts revenue, or protect the programme time your beneficiaries need?

A preview: later in this course, we will extend the double bottom line to the triple bottom line — adding environmental sustainability as a third dimension of accountability. For now, the dual commitment to financial and social performance is complex enough to command our full attention.

Mission-Market Tension: The Defining Challenge

The double bottom line is not just an accounting framework — it is a source of what Smith, Gonin, and Besharov (2013) call social-business tensions. Their landmark paper provides the most systematic scholarly treatment of these tensions, categorising them across four domains:

  • Performing tensions: Divergent goals and metrics. Success in financial terms (revenue growth, profitability) may conflict with success in social terms (depth of impact, reach to hardest-to-serve populations).
  • Organising tensions: Conflicting structures and processes. The operational efficiency a business demands may clash with the flexibility and patience that social programmes require.
  • Belonging tensions: Competing identities and values. Staff hired for commercial expertise may hold different values than staff hired for mission expertise. Founders themselves may feel torn between their identities as businesspeople and as social change agents.
  • Learning tensions: Different time horizons and knowledge demands. Markets reward speed and iteration; social change often requires long-term commitment and deep contextual understanding.

Smith et al. (2013) draw on paradox theory to argue that these tensions are not problems to be solved but paradoxes to be managed. They cannot be permanently resolved — they must be navigated continuously, with each decision recalibrating the balance. This is why the most experienced social entrepreneurs do not describe their work as having "figured out" the tension. They describe it as an ongoing practice of judgment, negotiation, and strategic compromise.

Tension in Practice: A Singapore Illustration

Consider a scenario drawn from the realities of Singapore's social enterprise landscape. A café-model social enterprise — let us call it Groundwork — trains and employs adults recovering from mental health conditions. Groundwork has achieved steady revenue through neighbourhood foot traffic and a few corporate catering contracts. Then a major bank approaches with a proposal: a twelve-month exclusive catering partnership worth three times Groundwork's current annual revenue. The catch? The bank needs guaranteed service levels that would require Groundwork to hire experienced commercial staff and reduce training hours for beneficiary employees.

This is mission-market tension in its purest form. The financial opportunity is transformative — it could fund programme expansion for years. But accepting it means temporarily compromising the very activity that defines the organisation's social mission. Declining it means forgoing security and growth. There is no clean answer. There is only a decision, made with imperfect information, that reflects the founder's judgment about which risk is more tolerable.

Think About It

Have you already faced a version of mission-market tension in your own venture? What did you decide — and on what basis? If you haven't yet, what decision do you anticipate will force this tension to the surface?

The Singapore Definition: What Gets Counted

Definitions are never neutral. When a government defines "social enterprise," it creates a boundary that determines who receives support — grants, tax incentives, capacity-building programmes, procurement preferences — and who is excluded. Singapore's definition, operationalised through raiSE, deserves careful scrutiny.

raiSE requires that a social enterprise demonstrate: a sustainable business model where the majority of revenue comes from the sale of goods or services; a commitment to the double bottom line; and a clearly identified social gap and disadvantaged community being addressed. For the "Leading Social Enterprise" tier, the bar rises further: annual revenue above S$250,000 and allocation of at least 20% of resources to intentional, human-centred social impact (raiSE, n.d.).

This definition is pragmatic and institutionally coherent. It aligns with Singapore's broader governance philosophy — results-oriented, measurable, commercially grounded. But it also creates blind spots. Ventures in early stages that have not yet reached S$250,000 in revenue may struggle to access ecosystem support. Organisations using non-traditional revenue models — cooperatives, community-owned enterprises, platform models where value flows to users rather than the entity — may not fit neatly into the framework. And the emphasis on "disadvantaged community" may inadvertently narrow the scope of what counts as social impact, potentially excluding ventures focused on environmental sustainability, civic participation, or cultural preservation.

Defourny and Nyssens (2010) would recognise this as a characteristically American-influenced approach: emphasising earned income and market sustainability. The European tradition, by contrast, would ask additional questions about governance — who controls the enterprise? Do beneficiaries have a voice in decision-making? Is profit distribution constrained? These are not merely academic distinctions. As Singapore's social enterprise ecosystem matures and engages more deeply with ASEAN neighbours — where cooperative traditions, informal economies, and community-based models are prevalent — the limitations of any single definition will become increasingly apparent.

Locating Yourself

This chapter has covered substantial conceptual ground: the definition of social entrepreneurship, its boundaries against adjacent concepts, the spectrum of hybrid models, the double bottom line, and the tensions that emerge when two bottom lines collide. These are not abstract ideas. They are the operating realities of the ventures you are building.

As Klarin and Suseno (2023) document, hybridity — the combination of commercial and social welfare logics within a single organisation — has become the central organising concept in contemporary social entrepreneurship scholarship. Your venture is, by definition, a hybrid. The question is not whether you will face tensions between your commercial and social commitments. The question is whether you will navigate those tensions with clarity, intentionality, and a framework robust enough to guide you when the easy answers run out.

The social enterprise spectrum, the double bottom line, and the mission-market tension framework are your starting tools. In the chapters ahead, we will layer onto these foundations: business model design, legal structures, impact measurement, funding strategies, scaling decisions, and the specific institutional landscapes of Singapore and ASEAN. Each new layer will return to the concepts introduced here and demand that you engage with them at a deeper level of sophistication.

For now, the task is foundational: know where you stand, know what you are accountable for, and know what will pull you in different directions. The space between profit and purpose is not empty. It is where the hardest and most consequential decisions in social entrepreneurship are made.

Key Takeaways

  • Social entrepreneurship is the innovative pursuit of social mission through market-oriented strategies — distinct from CSR (which remains profit-primary), charity (which lacks market orientation), and conventional startups (which lack mission primacy).
  • The social enterprise spectrum is a continuum from purely commercial to purely philanthropic, with social enterprises occupying hybrid positions that combine both logics in different proportions.
  • The double bottom line — simultaneous accountability for financial performance and social impact — is the defining feature of social enterprises and the source of their most challenging decisions.
  • Mission-market tensions are not problems to be solved but paradoxes to be managed, manifesting across performing, organising, belonging, and learning domains.
  • Singapore's raiSE definition provides a pragmatic institutional framework but carries assumptions that may exclude early-stage, cooperative, or non-traditional social enterprise models — a limitation that matters as the field engages with ASEAN's diverse institutional contexts.
  • Your venture already sits somewhere on the spectrum. Knowing where — and understanding what tensions that position creates — is the first step toward navigating them with intentionality.

Looking Ahead

In Chapter 2, we move from defining social entrepreneurship to examining the institutional ecosystems that enable or constrain it. How does Singapore's policy environment — from government grants to procurement preferences to the role of intermediaries like raiSE — shape what social enterprises can become? And how do these structures compare across the ASEAN mosaic, where the rules of the game vary dramatically from Manila to Yangon to Jakarta? You will begin mapping the specific ecosystem your venture operates within — and identifying the gaps where support is missing.
